books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Fourteenth Amendment to the Constitution, Section 2 (ratified 1868)

stimulus.text:
“Representatives shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers, counting the whole number of persons in each State, excluding Indians not taxed. But when the right to vote at any election for the choice of electors for President and Vice-President of the United States, Representatives in Congress, the Executive and Judicial officers of a State, or the members of the Legislature thereof, is denied to any of the male inhabitants of such State, being twenty-one years of age, and citizens of the United States, or in any way abridged, except for participation in rebellion, or other crime, the basis of representation therein shall be reduced...”

—Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868
stimulus.source_note: Fourteenth Amendment, Section 2, ratified 1868. Public domain. Wording verified against the Constitution Annotated (Congress.gov). Trailing ellipsis marks omitted text.

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: The split over the Fifteenth Amendment led Stanton and Anthony to form the National Woman Suffrage Association in 1869, while Stone and Blackwell formed the American Woman Suffrage Association. That split best shows that

options.text: the women’s movement agreed on every goal it held.
options.misconception: Background: two rival organizations is the opposite of agreement.

options.text: Reconstruction settled the question of women’s rights.
options.misconception: Background: the women’s question stayed open for fifty more years, until 1920.

options.text: even Reconstruction’s allies disagreed over accepting a partial victory.
the Fifteenth Amendment gave women the vote.
options.misconception: Background: the amendment gave women the vote nowhere.

rationales.A: Background: two rival organizations is the opposite of agreement.
rationales.B: Background: the women’s question stayed open for fifty more years, until 1920.
rationales.C: Both sides wanted women’s suffrage and supported Reconstruction. They split over one question: should a movement accept a victory that leaves its own members out? The two organizations are that disagreement, made permanent.
rationales.D: Background: the amendment gave women the vote nowhere.
rationales.general:
1. Two rival suffrage groups formed in the same year, 1869.
2. Both wanted the vote for women, and both backed Reconstruction.
3. Background: they differed over the Fifteenth Amendment, one side refusing a partial victory and the other accepting it.
4. So the split was not about ends, but about how much victory to take at once.
Remember: a movement can split over timing while agreeing on everything else.
